chapter_theme: One song at Aykudi (ஆய்க்குடி): seeing that the glory of conquering kings ends in a moment at the burning ground, the poet asks, like the devotees who left household life, to be done with the dance of birth; the praise tells of Siva kicking Death for the boy.

978.reading: Seeing that the great life of kings whose swords put armies to flight goes in a moment to the burning ground, the poet asks whether he may not, like the devotees who left household life and rose, look on the flower feet, rest from his weariness, and end the dance of coming into the world in a karma-strung body. The praise tells of Siva leaping with his anklet to kick the fierce form of Death when its noose struck at a boy, names Indra and the gods bowing, and calls Murugan the guardian of Aykudi who imprisoned Brahma and shattered the demons and the mountain by the sea with his vel.
978.nuance: The plea draws its lesson from the fall of kings, not from courtesans: மாத்திரைப் போதில் இடுகாட்டினில் போம், gone in an instant to the cremation ground, and its model is the renunciant (இல்வாழ்க்கை விட்டு ஏறும் அடியவர்). The boy and the noose are the story of Markandeya; the kick is Siva's, not Murugan's. The plea's last lines (கோப்புடைத்தாகி அலமாப்பினில் ...) are hard to divide.

links.note: Both take the death of kings as the proof of impermanence: the Naladiyar's kings under moon-white umbrellas are carried off, and 978's sword-bearing kings reach the burning ground in a moment; 978 draws from it the renunciant's resolve to end birth.

source_issues: Song 978: unflagged garble in வெருபக் (line 6), which seems to have lost a syllable.
